turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, I really think I can handle my own affairs and decide for myself who I'll marry.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not impressed by your connections, Mr. Worthing. A house in Belgrave Square is hardly the most desirable address, and I would have thought you would have had the decency to conceal your humble origins from my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I must correct you, Lady Bracknell. My family's circumstances are not quite as... humble as you might think.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you are not making a suitable impression, Mr. Worthing. I expect to see more substance and less... fabrication from a gentleman seeking to marry my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I am not making anything up. I am simply trying to give you an accurate account of my family's history.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Worthing, that your attempts to conceal your true nature are quite... amateurish.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, but I must insist that my family's reputation is not as tarnished as you seem to believe.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your defense of your family's reputation is quite... feeble. I shall not be swayed by your feeble attempts to justify their dubious past.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand that my family's past may not be perfect, Lady Bracknell, but I implore you to consider the good qualities I possess that would make me a suitable husband for your daughter.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that a man of your... questionable background would be a most unsuitable match for my daughter, Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I beg of you, Lady Bracknell, do consider the love I have for your daughter, Gwendolen. I assure you that I would do everything in my power to make her happy and provide for her well-being.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to be judged by my mother's prejudices, Jack. I know your character, and I will not be swayed by her doubts.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must remind you, Mr. Worthing, that a man's character is not defined solely by his feelings towards a particular young lady.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I would be most grateful if you could speak with your daughter, Lady Bracknell, and ask her if she still intends to marry me, despite your reservations.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I am perfectly capable of speaking for myself, Mother. I will not be lectured on my own marriage prospects.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must inform you, Mr. Worthing, that your proposal of marriage to my daughter has left me with considerable doubts regarding your social standing and family connections.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I must explain, Lady Bracknell, that my family connections are not as...straightforward as they might seem. I come from a respectable background, but I've also had the benefit of a guardian who has seen me through a bit of a...complicated situation.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I've had enough of your questioning, Mother. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I will not be swayed by your doubts.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Worthing, your explanation is hardly satisfactory. I still have grave reservations about your family's reputation and your own dubious background.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, and I assure you that I am not ashamed of my past. I believe my experiences have made me a stronger and more responsible person, and I am confident in my ability to provide for Gwendolen.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
